historic_survey.survey: Progressive Era & Early Revival Styles Historic Context Statement (2023)
historic_survey.note: The Richard P. Doolan/Norman T. Larson Residence and Storefronts built in 1903 — an extremely rare Colonial Revival mixed-use building, with Palladian windows carrying projecting shelf mouldings, oval windows and a hipped roof.

historical_record.description: The Baird estate sold this 32.5-by-100-foot corner lot, with other Haight Street parcels, to Richard P. Doolan, who built on it two years later.
The shop at 1508 Haight was a barbershop until 1967, from 1936 as the Haight Family Barber Shop.
The residence was turned into the Lansdorff Apartments.
The upper floors became the Evelyn Apartments, three units; the name survives in gold letters (restored) in the entry transom.
Jimmy's Shoe Shine Parlor worked from the 7½-foot-wide shop at 1504 Haight until 1975.
Holcombe Jewelers occupied the corner shop at 1500 Haight until 1988.
By 1953 the residence had been divided into eight living units, most likely during the Second World War housing shortage; it was a rooming house from the 1930s to the 1960s.

The Mnasidika clothing boutique traded in this storefront from 1965 to 1968; reportedly the first hip clothing store in the neighbourhood and instrumental in the Haight-Ashbury's development as a hippie enclave.

The Doolan-Larson Building at the corner of Haight and Ashbury, San Francisco Landmark No. 253 as the Richard P. Doolan / Norman T. Larson Residence and Storefronts, and one of the buildings associated with the counterculture era.
From 1968 the residence has legally been a single dwelling unit.
The property passed out of the Doolan family.
After standing empty in the early 1970s, the three shops at 1508-1512 Haight were merged behind a new front into one store, the Silmi Market, numbered 1510.
The western building was restored to its original three shops, using a 1952 Assessor's photograph as a model, with brass corner posts copied from one surviving original.
The storefronts were rehabilitated, and a decorative iron gate was installed at the 557 Ashbury residential entrance.
The two flats were physically rejoined into a single dwelling and the pocket doors between foyer and formal parlor were restored.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 253, the Richard P. Doolan/Norman T. Larson Residence and Storefronts.

historical_record.headline: Exclusive: Building at one of S.F.’s most historic intersections is getting a transformation

historical_record.description: Built as a two-storey Colonial Revival house at the northwest corner of Haight and Ashbury, its first floor about six feet above the street, by the contractor Charles J. U. Koenig.

The house was raised six more feet and moved 22 inches east to the lot line so that a row of shops could go in beneath it, and a separate commercial building went up on the western part of the lot — a rare mixed-use Colonial Revival in the city. The first shop on the corner was the Gold Bar saloon, which closed with Prohibition.

Mnasidika's proprietor was Peggy Caserta, and Janis Joplin was among its customers; the shop's name was a coded lesbian reference to Les Chansons de Bilitis. Holcombe Jewelers and Jimmy's Shoe Shine Parlor, long-standing shops on the corner, outlasted the drug years that followed.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, with exceptional significance, for its direct association with the hippie movement at the corner that gives the neighbourhood its name, and as a rare Colonial Revival house over shops.
